Summary (auto): quick technical deep dive on OpenTelemetry integration for token-level metrics, KV cache visibility, batching effects on latency/throughput, quantization interplay, and constraints for a VPC/on-prem deployment. Action items captured at end.

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone thanks for joining, um, appreciate you taking the time, we'll kick off real quick. I'm Alex from Redwood, AE, and Priya our SE will drive the tech. could you do quick intros from Haven?
[00:12] Marta: yep hi i'm marta, lead on model infra for inference, mostly responsible for serving and cost targets.
[00:17] Devon: devon here, platform manager, i'll own net connectivity and VPC peering questions.
[00:21] Samir: samir, security and compliance, i'll vet encryption, kms, audit.
[00:25] Priya: great, thanks. goal for today is to show how Redwood surfaces token-level telemetry via OpenTelemetry, how KV cache hits show up, and what instrumentation we recommend for on-prem / VPC deployments to keep latency under your p95 target.

[00:40] Alex: quick context, Haven's ask in the deck was ~2k tokens/sec sustained, p95 latency < 300ms for short chitchat style prompts and strict data residency. correct?
[00:50] Marta: yep that's right. we also have to keep cost per 1k tokens below our current infra bill baseline.
[00:55] Priya: okay good. so high level: there are three observability pieces — metrics for token flow, traces for per-token spans (optional sampling), and logs/audit for request-level. we usually recommend both OpenTelemetry metrics and trace spans emitted at the runtime layer.

[01:20] [Priya slides referenced: "Redwood OTEL integration"]
[01:26] Priya: the runtime emits token-level counters: token_emitted.count, token_latency.ms (histograms), kv_cache.hit_rate, batch_size.distribution. these are exposed as OTEL metrics via OTLP/gRPC or HTTP. if you're running in a private VPC we can either ship to your collector or you point the collector at Redwood's ingest endpoint over a private link.
[01:46] Devon: question — for VPC/on-prem we need air-gapped option, we can't reach public ingest. do you support an on-prem OTEL collector that writes to the Redwood private control plane?
[01:55] Priya: yes, we have an on-prem collector package that can forward via mutual TLS to your dedicated Redwood Dedicated endpoint or to our private peering endpoint. if truly air-gapped we can package an offline collector that writes to S3 and a small uploader. there are tradeoffs on latency for the latter.

[02:15] Samir: important: KMS/HSM— we need to make sure keys never leave our control. can you describe how you integrate with customer KMS for model decryption and audit logs?
[02:24] Alex: short answer — for Private we support customer-managed KMS via AWS KMS or external HSM through KMIP. keys remain in your account; Redwood's runtime requests decryption tokens via short-lived grants. we'll include the security binder.
[02:34] Samir: ok we'll need the specifics (SAML/SSO audit trace, who can export logs), so please add that to next steps.

[02:45] [03:00] Priya: diving deeper on token spans — we can emit a span per request and optional child spans for each token generation step: decoder.step, kv_lookup, attention_kernels. that allows you to see time spent in KV cache lookup vs kernel execution. but beware overhead: full per-token spans at 1:1 can add 10–20% overhead if sampled at 100%. our recommendation is representative sampling (1%) and full metrics (histogram of token_latency).

[03:40] Marta: would token-level spans show kv cache misses specifically? we need to know when the KV fallback goes to model recompute.
[03:45] Priya: yes — we emit kv_cache.hit boolean and a tiny attribute kv_latency_ms. a miss will show a child span that indicates fallback, and the trace will show a larger decoder.compute span. sometimes the transcriber muddles names — you'll see "KVk cache" in some auto fields in older releases, sorry about that.

[04:05] Jonah: also worth noting quantization behavior — int8 paths reduce kernel time but can increase variance on tail latency due to cache alignment. when we ran quantized 8-bit on a long seq distribution we saw p95 jitter go up ~30ms compared to FP16, but throughput improved ~1.8x. we'll show sample numbers.

[04:30] [05:00] Priya: here's an example dashboard — left panel token throughput over time, mid panel kv_cache.hit_rate heatmap by model version, right panel p95/p50 token latency by batch size. you can correlate increases in batch_size with improved amortized GPU kernel time but also with p95 increases if batch wait time grows.

[05:30] Marta: do you have an example alert rule for when kv_cache.hit_rate drops below 80%? we want to trigger fallback to a higher-capacity model variant.
[05:38] Priya: yes: alert if kv_cache.hit_rate < 0.8 sustained for 2 minutes AND token_latency.p95 > 400ms. action is canary route shift to variant with warmer cache or increase dedicated capacity. we'll provide the rule snippet.

[06:00] Devon: connectivity again — for private we planned VPC peering and private link. will that preserve OTLP traffic entirely inside our network?
[06:08] Alex: yes, with private link your OTLP agent can talk to Redwood ingest over private connectivity. for Dedicated deployments we can also host collectors inside your subnet that write directly to the local control plane.

[06:25] Samir: audit logs — are they immutable? retention?
[06:29] Priya: audit logs for Private are stored in your account or in a dedicated retention bucket depending on configuration; we support WORM-like retention policies and export to your SIEM (Splunk/Datadog). retention and immutability configurable to meet SOC2/ISO requirements.

[06:45] [07:10] Priya: let's talk about batching — Redwood runtime does continuous batching: requests are collected into a batch window (configurable 1–20ms) and sent to GPU. smaller window => lower latency but lower GPU utilization. larger window => higher throughput and lower cost. we expose batch_time_ms and batch_size histograms to tune that.

[07:35] Marta: our traffic pattern is bursty — periodic spikes from convo sessions, median prompt length 120 tokens. what's a good starting batch window?
[07:43] Priya: for 120-token median and your target p95 300ms we usually start with 5ms window with dynamic autoscaling. we also recommend prefix caching for frequent conversation turns to reduce effective tokens generated.

[08:00] Jonah: prefix/KV cache — important nuance: the KV cache is keyed on prefix embeddings; when you have many slightly different prefixes (e.g., user metadata), the hit rate drops. a best practice is to normalize prefixes or use a shared session key to increase locality.

[08:18] Marta: we have multi-tenant session ids, might need to standardize.

[08:22] [08:50] Priya: quantization talk real quick — two levers: model-level quantization (int8/4) and kernel-level optimized paths. quantization reduces memory and can give you higher batching windows, but be careful with very short prompts where quantization decode variance can hurt p95. we can run a quick A/B to measure regen rate and hallucination differences.

[09:05] Devon: are regressions in quality tracked in the console?
[09:09] Priya: yes, Redwood Optimize ties quality monitors to prompt sets and evals — you can alert on a quality metric drift alongside performance metrics. we can hook into your eval harness.

[09:30] [10:00] Marta: sample numbers please — in your bench earlier what were p50/p95 numbers for FP16 vs int8 at 2k tokens/sec?
[10:06] Priya: shorthand: FP16 p50 ~ 45ms, p95 ~ 260ms; int8 p50 ~ 28ms, p95 ~ 290ms (with some jitter). those numbers vary by model family and kernel maturity. we'll run one with your exact token distribution.

[10:30] [11:00] Samir: does your telemetry capture token-level credit usage for billing? we need per-team cost allocation.
[11:06] Alex: yes — token accounting is in the console and we can export token-level usage per API key, per route. cost breakdowns by model and quantization profile are supported.

[11:20] Marta: how intrusive is the OTEL instrumentation? do we need code changes?
[11:24] Priya: minimal for HTTP/SDK users — SDK emits spans and metrics by default. for custom runtimes we provide a lightweight sidecar or lib that instruments the runtime loop. sidecar approach good for on-prem.

[11:40] [12:00] Jonah: small gotcha — older OTEL Collector versions had a bug where histograms lost exemplar labels on high cardinality tags, so we recommend using collector v0.79+ or our patched build.

[12:15] Marta: good to know, we'll check our collector inventory.

[12:20] [13:00] Priya: demo time — i'm going to share a live dashboard (note: transcript will have a brief mute while screen shared).
[13:05] [screen share noise — 13:05–18:40]
[18:45] Priya: back — you can see a synthetic run where we sent a steady 2k tokens/sec, kv_cache.hit_rate stabilized at 87%, batch_size mean 8, and p95 at 275ms. when we toggled quantization to int8, throughput climbed to 3.4k tokens/sec and p50 dropped but p95 crept up 30ms.

[19:10] Devon: what's the path for doing a private on-prem pilot? we'd want to test within our data center and verify private link + KMS + telemetry.
[19:17] Alex: typical pilot steps: 1) exchange network/IP blocks, 2) deploy Redwood collector in your subnet, 3) run a small model with your prompt set for 72 hours, 4) collect dashboards and security review. we usually run a 'pilot kit' repo.

[19:38] Samir: security review length? we have a formal vendor process.
[19:42] Alex: usually 2–3 weeks for SOC2 review plus technical review; we've done expedited reviews with SSO and mutual NDA. we'll provide the security binder and contact for legal.

[20:00] [20:30] Marta: regarding fallback policies — can Redwood ramp to a cheaper model variant automatically on capacity pressure? we prefer graceful degradation instead of hard errors.
[20:37] Priya: yes, Smart routing can fallback by policy: cost-first or latency-first. you can set threshold e.g. if queue length > X or p95 > Y then route to model-variant-2. OpenTelemetry metrics feed those thresholds.

[21:00] Jonah: small comment on KV eviction — if eviction rate rises you'll see kv_cache.evictions metric, and a negative correlation with hit_rate and p95. we recommend warmup jobs to pre-populate cache after rollout.

[21:20] Marta: can we run a warmup job that uses session keys to pre-warm the cache for critical users?
[21:26] Priya: yes, we provide scripts and a warmup API. we can coordinate one for the pilot.

[21:40] [22:00] Devon: about logs retention — we need 1-year audit logs in immutable storage. possible?
[22:06] Priya: yes, for enterprise packages and Private deployments there are retention options up to multi-year; logs can be pushed to your S3/GCS with lifecycle rules.

[22:20] Samir: compliance: do you support SAML SSO with SCIM provisioning and RBAC?
[22:26] Alex: yes all supported; we'll include detail in the security binder and a sample SCIM claim map.

[22:40] [23:00] Priya: let's outline the benchmark we propose for the pilot: ingest your prompt set, run 72-hour sustained test at target traffic, capture token_latency histogram, kv_cache metrics, any regen/hallucination rate, and quantify cost per 1M tokens across quantization profiles.

[23:22] Marta: sounds good. one more Q: do you capture per-token embeddings generation time separately? embeddings are used in our rerank flow.

[23:30] Priya: embeddings emit separate metric families (embed_time.ms, embed_throughput). those join in dashboards for reranker pipelines.

[23:45] [24:30] Alex: wrapping up, quick recap: we'll send security binder, OTEL collector config, sample alert rules, and a benchmark plan. Priya will run the KV stress test and share results. Haven will share prompt distribution and SLOs. schedule kickoff for 2026-05-20 — does that week work?

[24:55] Marta: yes week of 5/20 works.
[25:00] Samir: thanks all, please include contact for legal.

[25:10] Alex: will do. any last questions? (brief silence) ok thanks everyone.
